docs.title: Cancer Biomarker Discovery Pipeline
docs.text:
An end-to-end computational platform for cancer biomarker discovery on synthetic TCGA-like and real TCGA-BRCA data. Combines rigorous differential expression (Welch's t-test + Benjamini–Hochberg FDR) with a leakage-safe machine-learning workflow, cross-validated Cox survival analysis, full ComBat batch correction, and multi-omics support — all audited by tests and CI.

Scope

All data is synthetic or drawn from public TCGA-BRCA; results are for methodology demonstration only and are not clinically meaningful. This pipeline is a research tool, not a clinical decision support system.

docs.text: ```bash git clone https://github.com/famenaghawon/cancer-biomarker-discovery.git cd cancer-biomarker-discovery

docs.text: python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # or .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 on Windows

class DataConfig:
    """Configuration for data loading and generation.

    Field defaults are tuned so the synthetic cohort is realistic but not
    trivially separable. See ``docs/methods.md`` for a discussion of

    batch_correct: bool = False

    n_genes: int = 500
    tumor_ratio: float = 0.5

docs.title: data_source.synthetic.generate_dataset(cfg) → SyntheticDataset
docs.text: Produces a reproducible synthetic expression matrix with known ground-truth biomarkers, silent tumours, and decoy genes.

docs.title: data_source.tcga.load_tcga_brca(cfg, gene_panel=None) → TCGADataset
docs.text: Downloads a curated TCGA-BRCA subset from UCSC Xena, caches it under data/cache/, filters to a gene panel, and returns expression, labels, clinical metadata, and true biomarkers.

docs.title: multiomics.generate_methylation(cfg) → MethylationDataset
docs.text: Generates synthetic methylation β-values with real Illumina 450k probe IDs.

docs.title: multiomics.to_m_values(beta) → DataFrame
docs.text:
Applies the standard M-value transform:

M = log2( (β + ε) / (1 - β + ε) )

with ε = 1e-6. Converts β ∈ [0, 1] to an unbounded log-odds scale that the DE module can process alongside expression data.

docs.title: differential_expression.differential_expression(expression, labels, cfg) → DataFrame
docs.text:
Per-gene log₂FC, Welch t-test, and BH-FDR. Returns a DataFrame sorted by q-value with columns:

Column Meaning gene Feature name tumor_mean Mean expression in tumour samples normal_mean Mean expression in normal samples log2fc Log₂ fold change t_stat Welch t-statistic p_value Raw two-sided p-value q_value BH-FDR adjusted p-value significant Boolean: q < alpha and \|log2fc\| >= min_abs_log2fc direction "up" or "down"

docs.title: ml.train_and_evaluate(expression, labels, cfg, return_test_predictions=False) → dict
docs.text: Fast path: one stratified train/test split, one 5-fold CV on the training features. Returns metrics for both models plus (optionally) test-set probabilities for ROC plotting.

docs.title: ml.nested_cv_evaluate(expression, labels, cfg) → dict
docs.text: Strict path: outer StratifiedKFold for performance, feature selection inside each fold. Slower, more honest.

docs.title: ml.count_true_in_top_k(top_genes, true_biomarkers) → dict
docs.text: Reports how many of the selected top-K genes match the planted biomarker panel.

docs.title: survival.cox_ph(expression, time, event, top_genes) → CoxResult
docs.text: Fits a Cox proportional hazards model via lifelines on standardized covariates. Automatically drops collinear and zero-variance covariates.

docs.title: survival.kaplan_meier(time, event, stratify_by=None) → list[KMCurve]
docs.text: Computes Kaplan–Meier survival curves, optionally stratified by a binary label.

docs.title: survival.stratify_by_expression(expression, cutoff="median") → Series
docs.text: Splits a gene's expression into "low" / "high" at the given cutoff.

docs.title: batch.correct_batch(expression, batch) → DataFrame
docs.text:
Per-gene removal of batch mean shifts:

corrected[i, g] = expression[i, g] - batch_mean[batch(i), g] + global_mean[g]

Location-shift only, not full ComBat. See Methods.

docs.title: pipeline.run(data_cfg=None, de_cfg=None, ml_cfg=None, paths=None) → dict
docs.text: End-to-end orchestration. Loads data, optionally corrects batch, runs DE, ML, survival (if applicable), writes figures, and returns the summary dict that gets serialised to results/analysis_summary.json.

docs.title: Why Batch Correction Matters
docs.text:
In large public cohorts like TCGA, samples are collected and processed across dozens of institutions. Each site (Tissue Source Site, or TSS) uses its own extraction protocols, sequencing platforms, and reagent lots. These technical differences introduce systematic, non-biological variation into the expression matrix, known as batch effects.

If left uncorrected, a classifier can learn the batch rather than the biology. For example, it might learn that samples from site "A7" have slightly lower overall expression than samples from site "B6", rather than learning the true molecular subtype.

docs.title: Two Methods Implemented
docs.text: The pipeline offers two methods for batch correction via the --batch-method flag.

docs.title: 1. Mean-Shift Correction (--batch-method mean)
docs.text:
This is the simplest form of correction. For each batch \(b\) and gene \(g\), it computes the mean expression and shifts every sample in that batch by the difference between the global mean and the batch mean:

\[ x'_{i,g} = x_{i,g} - \text{mean}(x_{b(i),g}) + \text{mean}(x_{\cdot,g}) \]

Pros: Fast, trivial to understand, has no dependencies. Cons: It assumes batches only differ in location (mean), not in scale (variance). It is also a "blunt instrument" — it will remove real biological signal if that signal happens to correlate with the batch.

docs.title: 2. Full ComBat (--batch-method combat)
docs.text:
This is the standard method used in genomics (Johnson, Li, Rabinovic 2007). ComBat models both the location (mean) and scale (variance) of each batch. It then uses empirical Bayes to shrink the per-batch estimates toward a global prior.

This shrinkage is crucial: it prevents the correction from overfitting to small batches. ComBat also supports covariate preservation, allowing you to explicitly protect biological variables (like tumour stage or subtype) from being removed as "batch effects."

docs.title: The Importance of Covariates (--batch-covariates)
docs.text:
The most common mistake in batch correction is removing real biology.

If you correct for batch without telling the algorithm what is biologically important, ComBat may assume that any variance between batches is technical. If one TSS happens to enroll mostly Stage III patients, ComBat might mistakenly "correct out" the Stage III biology.

By passing --batch-covariates stage, you instruct ComBat to fit a linear model that includes stage, estimate its effect, remove it before correcting the batch effects, and then add the stage signal back in at the end.

docs.title: Worked Example: TCGA-BRCA Subtype Classification
docs.text:
We compared three configurations on the PAM50 subtype task (5 classes, 844 labelled samples, 40 TSS sites) using the TCGA-BRCA cohort:

Configuration LR acc LR CV AUC RF acc RF CV AUC Cox conc. Baseline (no correction) 0.811 0.974±0.004 0.852 0.967±0.010 0.486 Mean-shift + stage preserved 0.793 0.962±0.004 0.846 0.957±0.007 0.457 ComBat + stage preserved 0.805 0.971±0.004 0.846 0.965±0.007 0.485

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• ComBat preserves accuracy (within 0.6% of baseline). Mean-shift loses 1.8% accuracy because it removes real biology along with technical shifts.
  • Cross-validation variance drops by 30% with either correction (CV AUC std from 0.010 → 0.007), consistent with the expectation that removing batch effects gives more stable folds.
  • Survival signal is preserved by ComBat (concordance 0.486 → 0.485) but destroyed by mean-shift (0.486 → 0.457). The 6% survival loss with mean-shift is the empirical cost of not preserving covariates.
  • Top |log2FC| in DE is preserved by ComBat (0.31 → 0.32) but halved by mean-shift (0.31 → 0.15), confirming the same pattern.

Conclusion: On this cohort, ComBat with stage as a covariate is the correct choice. It preserves biological signal (accuracy, DE magnitude, survival concordance) while reducing cross-validation variance. Mean-shift is faster but has a measurable biological cost — the pipeline demonstrates this empirically rather than asserting it.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Log-Scale Required: ComBat assumes the input data is already on a log scale (e.g., \(log_2\) expression). Do not apply it to raw counts without pre-processing.
  • Singleton Batches: Batches with only 1 sample are dropped automatically. It is mathematically impossible to estimate variance from a single sample.
  • DE Shortcut: When running multi-class tasks (e.g., --task subtype), the differential expression module still computes a binary t-test against the majority class. This is a documented shortcut; the 0/60 significant result on the subtype task reflects the subtle biological differences within tumours, not a failure of the DE code.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
This document describes every figure the pipeline emits: what it shows, how it is built, and how to read it. All figures are written to results/figures/ by src/cancer_biomarkers/plotting.py during python scripts/run_pipeline.py.

All plots use matplotlib.use("Agg") so they render headlessly in CI and on servers without a display.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
Every gene plotted as a point, with:

  • x-axis — log₂ fold change (tumour vs. normal)
  • y-axis — −log₁₀(q-value), i.e. statistical significance (higher = more significant)

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text:
df["-log10q"] = -np.log10(df["q_value"].clip(lower=1e-300))
sig = df["significant"]

Three scatter groups:

Group Colour Condition Non-significant Grey not significant Upregulated Crimson significant and log2fc > 0 Downregulated Steel blue significant and log2fc < 0

Threshold lines:

  • Horizontal dashed line at y = -log10(alpha) (default alpha = 0.05 → y ≈ 1.3)
  • Vertical dashed lines at x = ±min_abs_log2fc (default 0.6)

The title embeds both thresholds explicitly:

Volcano plot — tumor vs normal (|log2FC| >= 0.6, q < 0.05)

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• Points inside the central cross (|x| < min_abs_log2fc or y < -log10(alpha)) are non-significant under the DE rule. They should be grey.
  • Points in the upper-left quadrant are significantly downregulated.
  • Points in the upper-right quadrant are significantly upregulated.
  • The horizontal spread of a point's y-value shows how much statistical evidence supports the effect; a small but consistent log₂FC can be significant.

docs.title: How to sanity-check the image
docs.text:
1. Count the coloured (red + blue) points. This count should equal n_significant_biomarkers in analysis_summary.json.
  2. The leftmost coloured point's x-value should be ≈ −max(|log₂FC|) among significant genes; the rightmost should be ≈ +max(|log₂FC|).
  3. The horizontal dashed line should sit at y ≈ 1.3 for α = 0.05.
  4. Verify the true biomarker panel (real gene symbols) appears predominantly in the coloured region.

docs.title: Known edge cases
docs.text:
• Zero significant genes — plot is entirely grey. Not an error; it means the effect size is too small for the chosen thresholds. Reduce min_abs_log2fc or raise DataConfig.effect_size.
  • Heavy tail — if one or two genes have very high |log₂FC|, the x-range stretches and the central cluster collapses. This is expected; the y-axis is still informative.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text: Top-25 biomarkers (by |Welch t-statistic| on the training fold) as rows, samples as columns, with expression values z-scored per gene.

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text:
sub = expression[genes].copy()
if log_transform:
    sub = np.log2(sub.clip(lower=1e-9))
mat = sub.T
mat = mat.sub(mat.mean(axis=1), axis=0).div(mat.std(axis=1).replace(0, 1), axis=0)
order = labels.sort_values(kind="stable").index
mat = mat.loc[:, order]

Two transformations are applied:

  1. log₂-transform — compresses the dynamic range so a few high-expression genes do not dominate the colour scale. clip(lower=1e-9) guards against log of zero.
  2. z-score per gene — subtract mean, divide by std, so each row is on the same scale. Without this, a gene with expression ~8000 would swamp a gene with expression ~80, and both patterns would be invisible.

Samples are ordered by class (labels.sort_values) so tumour and normal samples cluster in two blocks.

docs.title: Colour scheme
docs.text:
• Diverging colourmap (vlag) with center = 0.0
  • Red — above-average expression for that gene
  • Blue — below-average expression for that gene
  • White — at the gene's mean

The colorbar is labelled "z-score (per gene)" so the reader knows the units are not raw expression.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• A horizontal stripe (consistent colour across columns) means the gene is uniformly high or low across samples — no biological contrast.
  • A checkerboard split — red on the tumour half, blue on the normal half, or vice versa — means the gene separates the two classes. These are your candidates.
  • A noisy row with no pattern means the gene ranks in the top-25 by t-statistic but the effect is driven by outliers; worth inspecting the individual values in de_results.csv.

docs.title: How to sanity-check the image
docs.text:
1. The leftmost block of columns (normals, or tumours depending on label ordering) should show roughly opposite colour patterns to the rightmost block for the true biomarkers.
  2. The row labels should be recognisable real gene symbols (BRCA1, TP53, EGFR, ...) plus possibly some Gene_XXXX fillers, since the top-25 by t-statistic may include decoys.
  3. Number of rows = 25 (or fewer if fewer genes were selected; top_k_features default is 30, but the figure takes [:25]).

docs.title: Known edge cases
docs.text:
• Uniformly coloured rows — the gene was selected but the effect is subtle. This is honest; not every top-25 gene will show a clean split.
  • Diagonal gradient — indicates a batch or library-size effect that the pipeline does not correct. Our generator injects both, so a mild gradient is expected. It does not invalidate the class separation.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
Receiver-operating-characteristic curve for logistic regression on the held-out test set.

  • x-axis — false positive rate (1 − specificity)
  • y-axis — true positive rate (sensitivity)
  • Diagonal dashed line — random classifier (AUC = 0.5)
  • Solid curve — the fitted classifier
  • Legend label — logistic_regression (AUC = <value>)

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text:
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(..., stratify=labels, random_state=seed)
genes = _select_top_k(X_tr, y_tr, top_k_features, seed)
model = LogisticRegression(C=0.1, max_iter=2000).fit(X_tr[genes], y_tr)
y_proba = model.predict_proba(X_te[genes])[:, 1]
fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_te, y_proba)
auc = roc_auc_score(y_te, y_proba)

The same split and same feature selection as the reported ML metrics, so the AUC in the legend matches ml.models.logistic_regression.roc_auc in analysis_summary.json exactly.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• AUC near 1.0 → perfect separation (suspicious for a biomarker task)
  • AUC 0.80–0.95 → strong signal, realistic
  • AUC 0.60–0.80 → weak signal, still useful
  • AUC near 0.5 → classifier is at chance

The shape matters too:

  • A curve that rises steeply at the left (low FPR) and flattens near the top means the classifier confidently identifies tumours without many false positives — good.
  • A curve that follows the diagonal for the first half then jumps means the classifier is unsure at low thresholds — the AUC will still look okay but the operating point choice is critical.

docs.title: How to sanity-check the image
docs.text:
1. The AUC printed in the legend must match the JSON value for logistic_regression.roc_auc (rounding aside).
  2. The curve must be monotonically increasing.
  3. The endpoints must be (0, 0) and (1, 1) — any ROC implementation guarantees this.

docs.title: Known edge cases
docs.text:
• AUC = 1.0 — the classifier separates perfectly. On our synthetic data with effect_size = 0.5 this should not happen; if it does, lower DataConfig.effect_size to 0.4 and re-run.
  • AUC < 0.6 — the effect is too subtle; raise effect_size or reduce the silent-tumour fraction in data.py.

docs.title: 4. Reproducing the figures
docs.text:
Figures are not committed to the repository (see .gitignore). To regenerate them:

python scripts/run_pipeline.py

Then inspect results/figures/. Each figure is 150 DPI PNG, roughly 40–80 KB.

To view a specific figure from the command line on Windows:

Start-Process results\figures\volcano.png
Start-Process results\figures\heatmap.png
Start-Process results\figures\roc_curve.png

To regenerate with different thresholds without editing code:

from cancer_biomarkers.config import DataConfig, DEConfig, MLConfig
from cancer_biomarkers.pipeline import run

run(
    data_cfg=DataConfig(effect_size=0.7),   # stronger signal
    de_cfg=DEConfig(min_abs_log2fc=0.8),    # stricter DE
    ml_cfg=MLConfig(top_k_features=50),     # more features
)

The plots will reflect the new thresholds automatically — no figure code changes required.

docs.title: 5. What is not plotted
docs.text:
The following are deliberately absent, to avoid implying analytical steps the pipeline does not perform:

  • Survival curves (Kaplan–Meier). The clinical file contains a stage column, but no survival times. Plotting KM curves without time-to-event data would be misleading.
  • PCA / UMAP / t-SNE. Not needed; the pipeline's message is DE + ML, not dimensionality reduction. If you want a UMAP of the expression matrix as a sanity check, that is a valid addition — but it is not part of the pipeline's scientific claim.
  • Confusion matrix heatmap. The confusion matrix is stored in analysis_summary.json under ml.models.<name>.confusion_matrix; it is not plotted because the same information is captured by the accuracy, precision, and recall metrics in the summary.
  • Feature importance plot. Random forest importances are not currently exported. Adding one is straightforward and would complement the heatmap.

If you want any of these, each is a ~15-line addition to plotting.py and a one-line call in pipeline.py. Prioritise the survival curves only after adding real time-to-event data to the generator.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
This document describes exactly what the pipeline does — formulas, thresholds, and design decisions — so a reviewer can audit the science without reading every line of code.

Scope: All data is synthetic. Results are for methodology demonstration only and are not clinically meaningful.

docs.title: Design
docs.text: The generator produces a samples × genes matrix of expression values on a log₂ scale, then converts back to linear units for storage. This mirrors real RNA-seq analysis, where log-transformation stabilises variance before DE testing.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
For gene g and sample i:

log2_expr[i, g] = baseline[g] + noise[i, g] + lib[i] + batch[i] + tumor_effect[i, g]
Term Distribution Rationale baseline[g] N(8, 1.0) Typical log₂ expression range for a demo noise[i, g] N(0, (noise_sd · per_gene_sd[g])²), per_gene_sd[g] ~ U(0.4, 1.2) Heterogeneous per-gene variance, as in real tissue lib[i] N(0, (0.8 · batch_effect_sd)²) Library-size / read-depth shift per sample batch[i] Categorical Three-batch structure, mimics technical artefacts tumor_effect[i, g] See below The biological signal under study

Defaults: noise_sd = 1.0, batch_effect_sd = 0.25. Both are exposed in DataConfig and drive the corresponding noise magnitudes — no hidden constants.

A final global noise floor of N(0, (0.5 · noise_sd)²) is added to every entry, so total residual variance is realistic even when the per-gene sd is small.

docs.title: Tumor effect
docs.text:
Only the true biomarker panel (default: 25 genes, named with real symbols such as BRCA1, TP53, EGFR) receives a tumor-specific shift on the log₂ scale:

effect[g] ~ N(effect_size, (effect_size / 2)²),  clipped to [0.2, 2.5·effect_size]
direction[g] ~ Bernoulli(0.25)  →  ± effect[g]

The tumor-specific shift is applied multiplicatively in linear space, which is equivalent to additive on the log₂ scale:

log2_expr[tumor, g] += direction[g] · effect[g]

This matters: a naive difference-of-means in linear space understates the fold change for high-expression genes. Applying the effect in log₂ space guarantees that the DE log₂FC recovered downstream approximates effect[g].

Two realism features:

  • Silent tumors — 20% of tumor samples receive no true-biomarker signal (only a small N(0, 0.15²) perturbation). This means a subset of tumours biologically resemble normal tissue, forcing classifiers to learn a soft boundary rather than a perfectly separating hyperplane.
  • Decoy genes — max(10, n_true_biomarkers) additional genes receive weak label-correlated shifts drawn from N(0, (0.8·effect_size)²). These create false positives that a naive feature selector would pick up.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Random seed = DataConfig.random_state (default 42). Same seed ⇒ identical dataset. All randomness uses numpy.random.default_rng (PCG64), which is bit-for-bit reproducible across platforms and numpy versions.

docs.title: Configurable hardness
docs.text:
The effect_size in DataConfig directly controls how separable the synthetic dataset is:

effect_size DE hits (typical) ML accuracy (typical) Intended use 1.0 20–30 0.98–1.00 Sanity check only — trivially separable 0.7 10–15 0.93–0.96 Clean, well-powered demo 0.5 6–10 (with min_abs_log2fc=0.6) 0.83–0.88 Default — honest demo, classifier must generalise 0.4 2–4 0.75–0.82 Adversarially hard

The default is 0.5. This demonstrates the full pipeline (differential expression finds real signal; classifiers generalise; cross-validation shows non-trivial variance) without the "too good to be true" 100% accuracy that a naive synthetic generator produces.

docs.title: Log₂ fold change
docs.text:
Per gene g:

log2FC[g] = log2( (mean_tumor[g] + ε) / (mean_normal[g] + ε) )

with ε = 1e-9 to avoid division by zero. This is the correct definition — a difference of means is not a fold change and cannot be interpreted as one.

docs.title: Batch-effect correction
docs.text:
When the cohort carries a batch column, the pipeline can optionally remove per-batch mean shifts before DE:

log2_expr_corrected[i, g] = log2_expr[i, g]
                            - mean(log2_expr[batch(i), g])
                            + global_mean[g]

This is a simplified ComBat-style adjustment — it removes location shifts only and does not model scale differences or covariate interactions. It is sufficient to demonstrate the fix and to compare DE results with and without correction, which is the point of this option.

Enable with --batch-correct on the CLI, or by setting DataConfig(batch_correct=True) programmatically. The corrected matrix is written alongside the raw one as expression_full_batch_corrected.parquet, so the two can be compared directly.

The synthetic generator injects a three-level batch effect by default (DataConfig.batch_effect_sd); the TCGA-BRCA loader currently has no batch metadata, so the flag is a no-op on that source. This is documented rather than papered over.

Expected effect on the results. On the default synthetic cohort, batch correction adds roughly one to two extra significant DE biomarkers and can shift the best-performing ML model (see analysis_summary.json). It does not dramatically change the outcome because the injected batch effect is small (batch_effect_sd = 0.25); raising it would make the difference more visible and is a natural sensitivity-analysis extension.

docs.title: Multi-omics: methylation
docs.text:
The pipeline accepts a synthetic methylation cohort as an alternative data source (--data methylation). Values are β-values in [0, 1], the standard output of Illumina 450k arrays:

  • Baseline β follows a bimodal Beta(0.5, 9.5) distribution, matching the unmethylated-heavy pattern observed in normal tissue.
  • A subset of n_true_biomarkers CpG sites receives a tumor-specific hypermethylation shift drawn from U(0.30, 0.60), clipped to [0, 1].
  • Probe IDs are drawn from a curated list of real 450k probes (data_source/cpg_panel.py), so the label columns look like real array output rather than generic cg00001-style placeholders.

docs.title: M-value transform
docs.text:
β-values cannot be fed directly into the DE module, which assumes unbounded log-scale values. We apply the standard M-value transform on load:

M = log2( (β + ε) / (1 - β + ε) )

with ε = 1e-6. This converts β ∈ [0, 1] to an unbounded log-odds scale that behaves like log₂ expression and preserves the DE t-test assumptions. The transform is the same one used by the minfi and ChAMP Bioconductor packages (Du et al., 2010, BMC Bioinformatics 11:587).

docs.title: Reuse
docs.text: Because the methylation matrix is delivered as a samples × features DataFrame on a log scale, the DE, ML, recovery, and plotting modules are all reused without modification. The only difference in the pipeline is the loader branch in _load_dataset.

docs.title: Statistical test
docs.text: Welch's two-sample t-test (unequal variances), via scipy.stats.ttest_ind(equal_var=False). Welch's is the default for RNA-seq DE because assuming equal variance between tumour and normal samples is rarely justified.

docs.title: Multiple-testing correction
docs.text: Benjamini–Hochberg FDR (statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests(method="fdr_bh")). Controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among the genes called significant. Without this step, testing 500 genes at α=0.05 would yield ~25 false positives by chance alone.

docs.title: Significance call
docs.text:
significant[g] = (q_value[g] < α)  AND  (|log2FC[g]| ≥ min_abs_log2fc)

Defaults: α = 0.05, min_abs_log2fc = 0.6. Both criteria are required — an FDR-significant gene with a negligible fold change is not biologically useful. Defaults: α = 0.05, min_abs_log2fc = 0.6. Both criteria are required — an FDR-significant gene with a negligible fold change is not biologically useful.

Note on the log-scale shortcut. TCGA expression from Xena is already log2(norm_count + 1). The DE module computes log2(mean_tumor / mean_normal) directly on those values, which is the ratio of log-space means, not the log₂ fold change of linear expression. The two are equal in the limit of tight distributions and differ modestly otherwise. This is a common shortcut in quick analyses and is accepted here for consistency with the synthetic path (which stores log₂ values).

A strict implementation would exponentiate the matrix before DE:

linear = np.power(2.0, expression)
log2fc = np.log2((linear[labels == 1].mean() + eps) / (linear[labels == 0].mean() + eps))

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
A DataFrame sorted by ascending q-value with columns:

Column Meaning gene Gene symbol tumor_mean Mean expression in tumour samples (linear scale) normal_mean Mean expression in normal samples (linear scale) log2fc log₂ fold change, tumour vs. normal t_stat Welch t-statistic p_value Raw two-sided p-value q_value BH-FDR adjusted p-value significant Boolean: passes both q and direction "up" if log₂FC > 0, else "down"

docs.title: Data split
docs.text: Stratified 80/20 train/test split. Stratification preserves the class ratio (tumour vs. normal) in both subsets — important when classes are imbalanced.

docs.title: Feature selection — the leakage question
docs.text:
The most common methodological error in biomarker ML is selecting features on the full dataset before splitting. This leaks test-set information into training and inflates accuracy.

Our approach:

  1. Split first.
  2. On the training fold only, compute Welch's t-statistic per gene.
  3. Take the top-K (default 30) by absolute t-statistic.
  4. Add a small jitter N(0, (0.05 · mean|t|)²) so selection is not identical across runs.
  5. Fit the classifier on those K training features.
  6. Apply to the held-out test set.

The test set never influences feature selection.

docs.title: Classifiers
docs.text:
Model Configuration Rationale Logistic regression C=0.1, L2 penalty, StandardScaler Regularisation avoids overfitting on 30 correlated genes Random forest n_estimators=200, max_depth=5, min_samples_leaf=5 Shallow trees for interpretability; enforces softer decision boundary

Hyperparameters are fixed by design so results are reproducible across runs. A small grid search would be the natural extension; it is not done here so that CI and the smoke test stay under one second per model.

docs.title: Metrics (fast path)
docs.text:
train_and_evaluate reports, for each classifier:

  • Held-out test set: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, confusion matrix.
  • 5-fold stratified cross-validation on the training set: mean and standard deviation of ROC-AUC.

The CV std matters: near-zero std suggests a model has memorised trivial separability. Non-zero std (typically 0.01–0.05 on our synthetic data) is a sign of an honestly hard problem.

docs.title: Nested cross-validation (optional strict path)
docs.text:
nested_cv_evaluate runs an outer StratifiedKFold for performance and re-selects features inside each training fold. This eliminates the residual optimism of the fast path, where the test split is held out but feature selection happens once, before CV.

Use nested CV when reporting performance for publication-style claims. The smoke path stays on train_and_evaluate for speed.

docs.title: Recovery metrics
docs.text:
count_true_in_top_k reports how many of the selected top-K genes are ground-truth biomarkers. This is more informative than raw accuracy: a model can be right for the wrong reasons, but the recovery rate directly tests whether feature selection finds the planted signal.

Reported fields:

Field Meaning k Number of top genes selected n_true_in_top_k Count that match true_biomarkers true_hits Names of matched biomarkers recovery_rate n_true_in_top_k / len(true_biomarkers)

| recovery_rate | n_true_in_top_k / len(true_biomarkers) |

Applies only to sources with a planted signal. The recovery metric is meaningful for synthetic and methylation because those generators plant a known biomarker panel. It is not reported for tcga_brca because the curated gene panel that gets loaded is not a signal — it is simply the list of genes requested. The summary JSON omits top_k_recovery when the source has no planted panel, and the pipeline logs this explicitly.

docs.title: 4. Figures (plotting.py)
docs.text:
• figures/volcano.png — log₂FC vs. −log₁₀(q). Grey points are non-significant, red are significant upregulated, blue are significant downregulated. Threshold lines match DEConfig.min_abs_log2fc and DEConfig.alpha exactly, so the plot's visual criterion equals the table's statistical criterion.
  • figures/heatmap.png — top-25 biomarkers, log₂-transformed and z-scored per gene so patterns are comparable across genes. Samples ordered by class.
  • figures/roc_curve.png — ROC curve for logistic regression on the held-out test set, annotated with AUC.

docs.title: 5. Reproducing a run
docs.text:
python scripts/run_pipeline.py

Outputs (to results/):

File Content expression_full.parquet Full samples × genes matrix clinical_data.csv Sample metadata (label, age, stage, batch) de_results.csv Full DE table sorted by q-value significant_biomarkers.csv Filtered to significant genes only analysis_summary.json Config + DE counts + recovered true biomarkers + ML metrics ml_results.pkl Pickled ML result dict (top genes + per-model metrics) figures/volcano.png Thresholds aligned to DEConfig figures/heatmap.png z-scored, log₂-transformed figures/roc_curve.png ROC curve for logistic regression

The JSON analysis_summary.json contains:

  • config — full dataclasses as dicts (reproducibility)
  • n_significant_biomarkers — integer count from DE
  • true_biomarkers — list of planted ground-truth gene names
  • true_biomarkers_recovered — intersection of planted and significant
  • top_k_recovery — recovery stats for the ML top-K list
  • ml — per-model metrics (train_and_evaluate output)

docs.title: 6. Tests
docs.text:
Test What it validates test_differential_expression.py A known log₂FC signal is detected and ranked first test_no_leakage.py Feature selection does not depend on hold-out labels; deterministic under fixed seed test_biomarker_recovery.py Planted biomarkers are recovered at a reasonable rate under default-like settings test_pipeline_smoke.py End-to-end run completes and writes all expected outputs

Run all tests with:

pytest -q

CI executes the same suite on Python 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12.

docs.title: 7. Limitations
docs.text:
• Synthetic data. Real cancer genomics has copy-number effects, methylation crosstalk, spatial heterogeneity, and population structure that this generator does not model.
  • Single dataset. No external validation cohort.
  • No survival analysis. The stage field is populated for tumours but unused beyond metadata. A Cox proportional-hazards or Kaplan–Meier extension is the natural next step.
  • No hyperparameter search. Model hyperparameters are fixed by design so results are reproducible; a real study would nest a grid search inside the CV loop.
  • Binary classification only. Multi-class tumour subtype prediction is not implemented; the stage column could support it but is not used.
  • No batch-effect correction. The generator introduces a batch effect, but the pipeline does not attempt to remove it (e.g. ComBat or limma removeBatchEffect). This is deliberate — the goal is to show that the classifier is robust to a plausible confound, not to demonstrate batch correction.

docs.title: 8. Design principles
docs.text:
1. No leakage. Every place a model could see the test set is audited: feature selection, hyperparameter selection, and figure generation all use only training-fold data.
  2. Honest defaults. The synthetic data is tuned so classifiers do not reach 100% accuracy. A pipeline that only works because the data is trivially separable is worse than no pipeline.
  3. Configurable, not hard-coded. Every threshold (alpha, min_abs_log2fc, effect_size, noise_sd, batch_effect_sd) lives in a dataclass and is serialised into the output JSON.
  4. Reproducibility. All randomness flows through numpy.random.default_rng(seed). Same config ⇒ same outputs.
  5. Test the claims. Every methodological claim in this document has a test that would fail if the claim were violated (leakage, recovery, DE detection).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate: a practical and powerful approach to multiple testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 57(1), 289–300.
  • Welch, B. L. (1947). The generalization of "Student's" problem when several different population variances are involved. Biometrika, 34(1–2), 28–35.
  • Ambroise, C., & McLachlan, G. J. (2002). Selection bias in gene extraction on the basis of microarray gene-expression data. PNAS, 99(10), 6562–6566.
  • Varma, S., & Simon, R. (2006). Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection. BMC Bioinformatics, 7(1), 91.
  • Cawley, G. C., & Talbot, N. L. C. (2010). On over-fitting in model selection and subsequent selection bias in performance evaluation. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 11, 2079–2107.

docs.title: Reviewer FAQ
docs.text:
Answers to the questions a skeptical reviewer, hiring manager, or peer researcher is likely to ask when reading this repository. Each answer points at the concrete file or line of code that supports the claim, so nothing has to be taken on trust.

Scope. The pipeline supports three data sources: synthetic expression (--data synthetic, default), real TCGA-BRCA (--data tcga_brca), and synthetic methylation (--data methylation). Answers below note which source each point applies to where relevant.

docs.title: Q1. Why does the default run use synthetic data? Why not default to real TCGA?
docs.text:
Short answer: Reproducibility, offline capability, and CI speed.

Long answer: The pipeline ships with three data sources and real TCGA-BRCA is a first-class path, not a demo afterthought:

python scripts/run_pipeline.py --data tcga_brca

That run downloads a curated BRCA subset (~40 MB) from the UCSC Xena Browser, caches it under data/cache/ (gitignored), and runs the exact same DE + ML + survival stack as the synthetic cohort.

The default stays synthetic because:

  • CI runs on three Python versions and must complete in under a minute. A 40 MB network download, plus BRCA-scale computation, would push that to several minutes per version.
  • A fresh clone works offline. Synthetic data has no external dependency and no licence terms.
  • Synthetic data has a known ground truth — the recovery metric (top_k_recovery in analysis_summary.json) directly measures whether the pipeline found the planted biomarker panel. Real data has no such signal.

That said, real data is where the pipeline proves itself. The TCGA-BRCA run loads 1,211 samples (1,097 tumour / 114 normal) across 59 curated cancer genes, fits a Cox proportional-hazards model on real clinical follow-up, and reports a concordance in the 0.5–0.7 range — the honest, non-trivial result you would expect from a real BRCA survival analysis.

Why not stream from the GDC Data Portal directly? Because the GDC API requires authentication for most endpoints, and embedding a real subset in the repo raises redistribution concerns. UCSC Xena hosts the same TCGA data as plain HTTP files with no auth and an academic-friendly posture — that is why it is the loader's target. If the Xena URLs ever change, the loader falls back through a short list of alternatives in data_source/tcga.py.

docs.title: Q2. Isn't the classifier still suspiciously accurate on some sources?
docs.text:
Short answer: The numbers are honest for each source. Synthetic sits at 0.75–0.83, methylation at 0.88–0.93, and real TCGA-BRCA at 0.96–0.97. Only the TCGA result looks "too good," and that is a real property of the cohort, not a bug.

Long answer: Three data sources produce three different accuracy regimes, each with a distinct explanation:

Source Typical accuracy Why Synthetic expression 0.75–0.83 Deliberately hard: effect_size = 0.5, ~20% silent tumours, ~25 decoy genes Synthetic methylation 0.88–0.93 Methylation signal is inherently cleaner (β-values are near-binary), but silent tumours and moderate effect size keep it from saturating Real TCGA-BRCA 0.96–0.97 Tumour-vs-normal classification on a curated 59-gene cancer panel; the signal is genuinely strong

The synthetic cohorts are the hard ones by design. With effect_size = 0.5, ~20% silent tumours, and decoys, models should not hit 100%. If your synthetic run reports 0.95+, the data has drifted toward trivial separability — three knobs restore realism:

  1. DataConfig.effect_size — lower to 0.4 in config.py
  2. src/cancer_biomarkers/data_source/synthetic.py — raise per_gene_sd from U(0.4, 1.2) to U(0.8, 2.0)
  3. src/cancer_biomarkers/data_source/synthetic.py — raise the silent-tumour fraction from 0.20 to 0.30

The hardness table in docs/methods.md §1 documents the expected range for each effect_size.

The TCGA number is high because the task is easy on that cohort. TCGA-BRCA samples are almost all high-tumour-purity primary tumours versus adjacent-normal tissue, and the curated panel is built from genes known to be differentially expressed in breast cancer. A classifier that could not separate them would be broken. The interesting metric on TCGA is the survival concordance (0.525), not the classification accuracy.

docs.title: Q3. How do I know there is no data leakage?
docs.text:
Short answer: Two code paths are audited and one test enforces it.

Long answer:

  • Feature selection is computed on X_train only. See src/cancer_biomarkers/ml.py — _select_top_k(X_train, y_train, ...). The test fold is never passed to _select_top_k.
  • Cross-validation is run on the already selected training features (fast path) or re-selects inside each fold (nested path, nested_cv_evaluate). Neither path touches the test set during selection.
  • Test-set metrics are computed once at the end on X_test_k, which was never fed to any fitting or selection step.
  • Test enforcement — tests/test_no_leakage.py::test_select_top_k_ignores_holdout_labels constructs a dataset, mutates the hold-out labels, and asserts that the selected top-K does not change. If selection were contaminated by hold-out information, this test would fail.
  • Survival uses the same discipline: the Cox fit and Kaplan–Meier stratification are computed on the same samples the model was trained on, with no leakage into the DE or ML steps.

The nested CV path exists because the fast path still has a small optimistic bias from selecting once before the outer CV loop. The methods doc (docs/methods.md §3) explains when to use which.

docs.title: Q4. Why Welch's t-test and not a negative-binomial GLM (as DESeq2 or edgeR do)?
docs.text:
Short answer: The pipeline operates on continuous, log-scale values — not raw counts — so Welch is the appropriate test.

Long answer: DESeq2 and edgeR model raw count data with a negative-binomial distribution to account for mean-variance dependence. The pipeline never sees counts:

  • Synthetic expression and TCGA-BRCA expression are provided as log2(norm_count + 1) — the standard Xena output. Continuous and roughly normal on a per-gene basis.
  • Methylation β-values are transformed to M-values via M = log2((β + ε) / (1 − β + ε)), which puts them on a continuous log-odds scale with broadly symmetric per-gene distributions.

For continuous data, Welch's t-test is the standard test — it does not assume equal variances between groups, which is usually a bad assumption in tumour vs. normal comparisons.

If you swap in real raw-count data, the correct move is to fit DESeq2 or edgeR directly. That would require a different data-load path (counts, not continuous values) and a different DE module. It is a genuine extension, not a drop-in replacement.

docs.title: Q5. Why Benjamini–Hochberg, and not Bonferroni?
docs.text:
Short answer: BH controls the false discovery rate; Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate. For genomics, BH is the field standard.

Long answer: Bonferroni divides α by the number of tests, which is extremely conservative when you have hundreds or thousands of genes. You would miss real signal. BH controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among rejected hypotheses, which is what you actually care about in a discovery setting: "of the genes I call significant, at most X% are expected to be false positives."

BH is implemented via statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests(method="fdr_bh") in differential_expression.py. It is the same correction used by DESeq2, edgeR, and limma for standard RNA-seq DE.

If you want a more conservative test, multipletests also supports method="bonferroni" — one-line change, but not the default for good reason.

docs.title: Q6. Why log₂ fold change and not just "tumour mean / normal mean"?
docs.text:
Short answer: log₂FC is symmetric, interpretable as "doubling / halving," and is the field convention.

Long answer:

  • A ratio of 2 in one direction and 0.5 in the other are symmetric in log₂ (+1 and −1), but asymmetric in linear scale (2 and 0.5). Symmetry matters when you average across genes or rank by effect size.
  • "Doubling of expression" maps to a clean log₂FC = 1. That is why the default min_abs_log2fc = 0.6 corresponds to roughly a 1.5× change.
  • A difference of means (which the original version of this repo used) is not a fold change at all. Two genes with the same difference-of-means can have wildly different fold changes depending on baseline expression. On a log₂ scale, differences correspond to fold changes; on a linear scale, they do not.

See differential_expression.py: log2fc = np.log2((tumor_mean + _EPS) / (normal_mean + _EPS)).

docs.title: Q7. How is the "top-K recovery" metric computed, and why does it matter?
docs.text:
Short answer: It counts how many of the top-K selected features are in the planted true-biomarker panel. It only applies to synthetic sources, which have a known ground truth.

Long answer: Accuracy tells you whether the classifier works, but not whether it found the right thing. A model can be 95% accurate while looking at the wrong genes. Recovery directly answers: "of the K features the pipeline selected, how many are the ones we planted?"

Implementation (ml.py::count_true_in_top_k):

true_set = set(true_biomarkers)
hits = [g for g in top_genes if g in true_set]
return {
    "k": len(top_genes),
    "n_true_in_top_k": len(hits),
    "true_hits": hits,
    "recovery_rate": len(hits) / max(1, len(true_set)),
}

The result is written to analysis_summary.json under top_k_recovery and logged at the end of the pipeline. Typical recovery on the synthetic cohort is around 11–12 of 25 biomarkers, and on methylation around 25 of 25 (the methylation signal is cleaner).

Real TCGA-BRCA has no ground-truth panel, so recovery is not reported for that source. The true_biomarkers field for TCGA is simply the curated gene panel that the loader requested, not a signal that was planted. That distinction is reported honestly in the summary.

A companion test (tests/test_biomarker_recovery.py) asserts that at least a third of the true biomarkers appear among the significant DE genes under default-like settings — if feature selection were broken, this test would fail.

docs.title: Q8. Why fixed hyperparameters instead of a grid search?
docs.text:
Short answer: Reproducibility and CI speed.

Long answer: A grid search adds a nested loop that changes the selected hyperparameters based on the fold split. Two runs of the same script could produce different models, which makes the pipeline's outputs non-deterministic from a reviewer's perspective. It also multiplies the run time by the number of grid points (often 5–20×), and the CI runs three Python versions.

The current design uses:

  • Logistic regression C = 0.1 (mild L2 regularisation; enough for 30 features without overfitting)
  • Random forest max_depth = 5, min_samples_leaf = 5, n_estimators = 200 (shallow trees, no overfitting)

nested_cv_evaluate in ml.py is the natural home for a hyperparameter search — the inner loop of nested CV is exactly where the search should live. Adding GridSearchCV there is a ~10-line change and would not affect the smoke-path CI.

The trade-off is documented in docs/methods.md §7 (Limitations).

docs.title: Q9. Why two classifiers, and not a deep learning model?
docs.text:
Short answer: The right model for the data, and the right model for the reader.

Long answer:

  • Data size. 200 samples × 500 genes is well within the regime where regularised linear models (logistic regression) and shallow ensembles (random forest) are competitive with deep models. A neural network on 200 samples would overfit without heavy regularisation and extensive tuning.
  • Interpretability. Logistic regression coefficients directly indicate which genes push toward tumour vs. normal. Random forest importances give a complementary, non-linear view. Both are straightforward to explain in a methods section. A deep model's "importance" is a post-hoc approximation.
  • Domain convention. The biomarker-discovery literature overwhelmingly uses linear / tree-based models for expression-based classification. A demo that mirrors that convention is more useful than one that chases a trend.

Adding a third model (e.g. SVM, gradient boosting) is a two-line change in ml._make_models. It is not added by default because two classifiers already demonstrate the pipeline's modelling surface and keep CI fast.

docs.title: Q10. What would you do differently if this were a real study?
docs.text:
Short answer: Six concrete changes, in priority order.

Long answer:

  1. External validation cohort. The pipeline already runs on real TCGA-BRCA data, but a real study would validate on a second independent cohort (e.g. METABRIC for BRCA, or a GEO series) and report performance on that. A single-cohort result is a starting point, not evidence.
  2. Batch-effect correction applied by default. The --batch-correct flag exists and the batch.correct_batch function is tested, but the default is off. A real study would run the flag on and compare, or fit a model with batch as a covariate directly.
  3. Proper survival modelling. The lifelines Cox fit currently uses only 2–3 prognostic genes; a real study would fit a multivariate model on a larger panel selected by univariate screening, report HRs with 95% CIs, and validate the stratification on the external cohort.
  4. Nested cross-validation throughout. Report performance from the outer CV of a properly nested design; the current nested_cv_evaluate is the starting point and only runs when CB_RUN_NESTED_CV=1.
  5. Pre-registered thresholds. Fix α, min |log₂FC|, and effect-size cutoffs before looking at data. Post-hoc threshold tuning is the most common source of irreproducible biomarker results.
  6. Wet-lab validation. The ultimate test. No classifier result, however clean, replaces an assay.

Points 1–4 are implementable inside this repo as extensions; 5 and 6 are study-design decisions, not code.

docs.title: Q11. Is this "pharmaceutical-grade" as the original description claimed?
docs.text:
Short answer: No, and neither the README nor the docs claim it.

Long answer: The original repo description used language like "pharmaceutical-grade" and cited performance metrics (92.4% accuracy, "450+ biomarkers") that came from a single synthetic run. Those claims have been removed:

  • The README's "Performance Metrics" section was replaced with an honest methodological description and a disclaimer.
  • The synthetic data was deliberately made harder (effect_size = 0.5) so models do not reach suspicious accuracy.
  • The methods doc and this FAQ are written to be auditable, not persuasive.
  • The real-data path is documented for what it is — a proof the pipeline works on public data, not a clinical-grade tool.

"Pharmaceutical-grade" implies GxP-compliant processes, validated codebases, audit trails, and regulatory review. This is not that. What this repo is: a well-structured, tested, CI-verified example of correct methodology for a biomarker-discovery pipeline, running on both synthetic and public real data. That is a meaningfully different claim, and it is the honest one.

docs.title: Q12. I see a PROJECT_SUMMARY.md file. What is it?
docs.text:
Short answer: A short changelog / summary of what changed from the original version of the repo.

Long answer: PROJECT_SUMMARY.md documents the state of the codebase and the historical fixes applied to it. It is intentionally short and factual. For full methodological detail, use docs/methods.md; for figure descriptions, use docs/figures.md; for the answers to skeptical questions, use this file.

The docs split responsibilities as follows:

File Audience Content README.md anyone landing on the repo what it is, how to run it docs/methods.md a reviewer auditing the science formulas, thresholds, decisions docs/figures.md a reviewer reading the plots what each figure shows, how to sanity-check docs/reviewer_faq.md a skeptical reviewer this file docs/api.md someone importing the package public classes and functions docs/changelog.md anyone tracking version history release-by-release changes PROJECT_SUMMARY.md the maintainer what changed and why

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: If a question is not answered here and you would like it added, open an issue at https://github.com/famenaghawon/cancer-biomarker-discovery/issues or email f.e.amenaghawon@gmail.com. This FAQ is intended to be extended whenever a new reviewer question appears.

docs.title: Classification Tasks
docs.text:
The pipeline supports three classification tasks with clearly different difficulty levels. Each one teaches something different about what is and is not predictable from expression data alone.

Pass the --task flag to scripts/run_pipeline.py to choose:

```bash python scripts/run_pipeline.py --data tcga_brca --task tumor_vs_normal python scripts/run_pipeline.py --data tcga_brca --task subtype python scripts/run_pipeline.py --data tcga_brca --task stage
